newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Beazley's woes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Beazley's woes.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
Could the Lindsay by-election result really mean that the Labor Party was seven percent more popular under Paul Keating than it is under Kim Beazley?

A bizarre interpretation? Well, it's almost as valid as many of the other political theories being hung on the Lindsay vote, which saw the Liberals get a six percent swing towards their candidate, Jackie Kelly, and Labor see seven percent of the vote swing away from former minister Ross Free.
That was the outcome on primaries. The two-party result put the Libs up and Labor down by 4.76 percent.
A rapturous John Howard at the Liberal Party federal council dinner in Hobart was beside himself with delight.

On the night he simply welcomed the result as a just outcome: the voters had given Jackie Kelly the fair go the Liberals had called for after she'd been thrown out of the seat by the High Court on a constitutional technicality.
But overnight Howard's team developed the spin. It was, Howard said, a message to the Senate to "get out of the way" and let his programme through.
That got a big run in the media everywhere -- just the outcome the tacticians had in their sights.
But it might come as a bit of a surprise to the Lindsay voters, out around the western Sydney centre of Penrith.

It's more likely they were simply fed up with this voting nonsense. They had thrown Labor and Ross Free out just seven months earlier with an 11 percent swing; they had grown to like Jackie Kelly in that short time and they were telling Canberra that they meant their March vote. They were telling all politicians to "get out of their face". In short, too much democracy was more than enough, thank you very much.
But while the Liberals were pinning extra messages onto the result, Labor's Kim Beazley was attempting the truly unbelievable, declaring the result meant "nothing."

Presumably, that's because he simply couldn't face the truth. Far from "nothing", the result meant that Labor had gone backwards since March. A budget full of nasties, a couple of weeks of parliamentary mayhem, two front benchers resigned. None of that counted to the electors of Lindsay.
Labor's morale is shot. Recriminations abound. The New South Wales Right, accustomed to dishing out the blame, has been forced to take it.

Ross Free convinced the party's New South Wales secretary, John Della Bosca, that it should pursue Jackie Kelly's failure to resign from the air force in time, under the constitutional ban on candidates being in offices for profit under the crown.

National secretary Gary Gray opposed the challenge, as did almost everyone else. But Gray didn't press the point with his New South Wales counterpart. The trouble is, the party has suffered nationally, not just in New South Wales.

That's why Beazley should have followed his inclination against the challenge. But he let Della Bosca have his head. It's Beazley's natural game to give way to those who argue more forcefully -- that is, the New South Wales Right.

Some party members are putting this together with recent behind-the-scenes activity on the parliamentary front. In the recent ministerial shares, debate Laabor was on the front foot on all but one day.
The exception was the day when deputy leader Gareth Evans insisted on pursuing Peter Costello about his wife's shares.

Simon Crean thought this would be a tactical mistake and argued the case in the strategy meeting before question time. Evans persisted and Beazley acquiesced. As a result, Costello lambasted Labor and the advantage was lost.
This tendency is starting to raise questions about the strength of Beazley's leadership, although it's much too early to say that there are any serious rumblings within the party.

But Howard and his front bench are making every post a winner. At strategic parliamentary moments, they have been goading Beazley and Evans about how well Crean is performing from the opposition front bench.
That would work only if there were more than a grain of truth in the taunts. And there is.

Crean, as Labor's manager of business in the house, has found unexpected form. His explanation is that while Beazley and Evans were there in opposition before 1983 and do not appreciate a return visit, Crean entered parliament in 1990 -- straight into government. Opposition is just a new experience and he's enjoying the freedom.
But Beazley needs to think deeply about his leadership style. It might be only whispers now but these things always have small beginnings and the warnings should be heeded.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2370
